pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 with answers to three decimal places, understanding that the DIGITS shift position in the place-value chart (the point moves nowhere; the digits move).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — explain patterns in the number of zeros / placement of the decimal point when multiplying or dividing by powers of 10; extends 5.NBT.1 (a digit in one place is 1/10 of the place to its left).
• Operational details — secure the concept that ×10 shifts every digit ONE place to the LEFT (each digit becomes ten times bigger) and ÷10 shifts every digit one place to the RIGHT; ×/÷100 = two places, ×/÷1000 = three places. The decimal point is a fixed marker of the ones place; it is the digits that travel. Zeros are placeholders that appear to fill vacated places (0.0452), never 'just add a zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly, describing it as digits moving two places left. Tier B (10–11): 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452, inserting placeholder zeros correctly. Tier C (11): explain WHY ×10 shifts each digit one place left in terms of each digit becoming ten times its value.
bestPractices: Teach 'digits move, the point stays' explicitly and BAN 'add a zero / move the decimal point' — the add-a-zero rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40) and mispositions the point; the movement-of-digits image generalises correctly.
Use a place-value chart (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths) and physically SLIDE digit cards left/right across the columns, so the shift is enacted, not stated.
Connect ×10 and ÷10 as inverse shifts (left ↔ right) and chain them (×100 = ×10 then ×10) so the size of the shift maps to the power of ten.
Confront placeholder zeros head-on: when ÷1000 empties the ones and tenths columns, a 0 must hold each empty place (0.0452), and the leading zero before the point is written by convention.
Ground WHY in place value (5.NBT.1): a digit is worth ten times the digit one place to its right, so making a number ten times bigger moves every digit into the next-higher column.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding digit cards spanning thousands to thousandths and the decimal point fixed at the ones boundary.
Left/right shift arrows annotated with the power of ten (×10 = 1 left, ×100 = 2 left, ÷1000 = 3 right).
Gattegno chart (rows of ×10 scaling) to show a digit jumping between rows as it is multiplied/divided by powers of ten.
Zoom / 'ten-times' number line to reinforce that ×10 makes the whole quantity ten times as large, not merely longer to write.
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero when you multiply by 10' — wrong for decimals (2.5 × 10 ≠ 2.50) and a source of place-value damage.
'Move the decimal point' — leads to moving the point the wrong way or mispositioning it; the point is fixed, the digits move.
Omitting placeholder zeros when dividing (45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 or .0452 rather than 0.0452).
Confusing the DIRECTION: multiplying making the number smaller (shifting right) or dividing making it larger.
Shifting only one digit or the wrong number of places, especially for ×/÷1000 (three places).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 (answers up to three decimal places, with 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 as a four-decimal-place extension) by understanding that every DIGIT shifts position across the place-value chart while the decimal point stays fixed at the ones boundary. The organising principle is 'digits move, the point stays'; ×10 shifts each digit one column left (each digit becomes ten times bigger), ÷10 shifts one column right, and the number of places matches the number of zeros in the power of ten. Placeholder zeros fill vacated columns (e.g. 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452). This counters the 'just add a zero' habit, which breaks for decimals, and gives a place-value reason for 'move the point', which gets correct answers but is often learned without understanding.

activities.title: Slide the digits across a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.456 × 100 = 3.45600, point out the value has not changed at all and the digits sit in the same columns — ask them to slide each digit two columns left instead so 3 lands in the hundreds, giving 345.6.

If 45.2 ÷ 1000 comes out as 0.452, have them count every column each digit crosses and check that each written emptied column (ones and tenths) holds a 0, giving 0.0452. If it comes out as .0452, note that the value is correct but the conventional 0 in the ones place should be written: 0.0452.
If a learner shifts the wrong way, ask whether the number should get bigger (×, shift left) or smaller (÷, shift right) and re-slide.

If the shift is in the right direction but off by one place, have them match the count to the number of zeros in the multiplier/divisor and recount; if the error repeats, check whether they are counting the decimal point or digits instead of columns.
activities.rationale: The target concept is literally a movement of digits across place-value columns, so enacting the slide (physically or on screen) with the point held fixed is intended to make 'digits move, the point stays' something the learner performs rather than recites, and dividing to a leading-zero answer forces the placeholder-zero reasoning that the 'add a zero' rule hides.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns from thousands down to ten-thousandths, with the decimal point marked fixed at the ones boundary (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths ten-thousandths); the extra low columns are needed because 45.2 ÷ 1000 lands a digit in the ten-thousandths place.
Write 3.456 into the chart using digit cards, then multiply by 100: slide EVERY digit two columns to the LEFT in one move, keeping the point pinned in place, to land on 345.6.

Now take 45.2 and divide by 1000: slide every digit three columns to the RIGHT (the tenths digit travels into the ten-thousandths column), and write a placeholder 0 into each emptied column that is written (ones and tenths) to get 0.0452.
Say aloud for each step: 'the digits moved ___ places ___ because I multiplied/divided by ___', linking the number of places to the power of ten.
Try a target challenge: starting from 3.456, work out which single operation reaches 345.6, and which reaches 0.3456.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten moves every digit a fixed number of place-value columns while the decimal point stays put; the number of columns equals the number of zeros in the power of ten, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Why ten-times moves each digit one column
feedback: If a learner treats ×10 as 'making the number longer', redirect to the quantity itself being ten times as large — 2.5 × 10 is twenty-five, not 'two point five oh'.
If they cannot say why the shift is one column, revisit that each column is ten times the one to its right, so a ten-times-bigger value lands one column left.
If they struggle to connect the power of ten to the number of places, have them break ×100 into ×10 then ×10 and count the columns.
activities.rationale: Grounding the procedure in place-value structure (each place is worth ten times the place to its right) is intended to turn a memorised rule into explained behaviour, which may support transfer to ×/÷1000 and help learners resist the 'add a zero' shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10; a digit represents ten times the place to its right.
Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Pick a digit in a number, e.g. the 4 in 3.456 (worth four tenths), and state its value.
Explain why, when the whole number is made ten times bigger, that digit must now be worth ten times as much (four ones) and therefore move one column to the left.
Use a scaling chart or a 'ten-times' number line to show the whole quantity becoming ten times as large, not merely gaining an extra written digit.
Chain the reasoning: ×100 is ×10 then ×10, so each digit moves one column left twice — two columns in total — and connect ÷10 as the exact inverse (one column right).
activities.intendedInsight: Because each place-value column is worth ten times the column to its right, making a number ten times bigger promotes every digit into the next-higher column; this is WHY the shift happens and why ×100 shifts two columns and ÷1000 three.

activities.title: Fluency and error checks
feedback: A missing-placeholder answer (0.452 for 45.2 ÷ 1000) should prompt counting every column and filling emptied ones — 0.0452.
An 'append zeros' answer (3.45600) should prompt re-sliding the digits two columns left.

An off-by-a-factor-of-ten answer should prompt the learner to recount places against the zeros in the operator; if it recurs, check how they are counting columns rather than assuming it is only a slip.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and fill-in tasks are efficient for checking fluency and catching recurring errors, though on their own they do not build the shift image — they complement the enacted chart work rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items such as 45.2 ÷ 1000 = ____ , writing all placeholder zeros, and 3.456 × 100 = ____ .
Answer direction questions: when dividing by a power of ten, which way do the digits move, and how many places for ÷1000?
Order a set of results by size, e.g. 2.5 × 10, 2.5 × 100, 2.5 × 1000, and explain the ordering by place-value shift.
Self-check each answer by counting the columns crossed against the number of zeros in the multiplier or divisor.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated practice with answers up to three decimal places (plus the four-decimal-place extension 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) is intended to make the power-of-ten ↔ number-of-places mapping more automatic and to surface the common errors (missing placeholder zeros, wrong direction, miscounting by one).

activities.title: Challenge the 'add a zero' habit through dialogue
feedback: If a learner cannot explain the error, have them place both 2.5 and the proposed 2.50 in a chart and compare values — they are identical, so no multiplication has occurred.
Confirm the correct answer (25) by sliding each digit one column left.
activities.rationale: Prompting a learner to diagnose a misconception out loud may consolidate understanding; this is a supporting discussion activity that can accompany, but does not replace, enacting the digit shift on a chart.
sourceClaims: Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim a friend might make: '2.5 × 10 = 2.50'. Explain exactly what has gone wrong and give the correct answer with reasoning.
Explain why 3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600, referring to where each digit sits in the place-value chart.
Describe, in your own words, when 'add a zero' happens to look right (whole numbers) and why it fails for decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'add a zero' rule is unreliable for decimals because it ignores place value. 'Move the point' gives correct answers, but used as a bare rule it hides why. Explaining the flaw is intended to strengthen the digits-move model.

constraints: Explicitly teach 'digits move, the point stays' and avoid 'add a zero' because it gives wrong results for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40). Do not lead with 'move the decimal point': it gives the same answers, but it hides the place-value reason, and the point is better treated as a fixed marker of the ones place.

Placeholder zeros must be confronted directly: when division empties columns, a 0 must hold each written vacated place (0.0452 has zeros in the ones — by convention — and tenths), and answers like 0.452 or .0452 should not pass unaddressed.
Match the number of places shifted to the power of ten (×/÷10 = one place, ×/÷100 = two, ×/÷1000 = three) and keep direction correct (× shifts left/bigger, ÷ shifts right/smaller).
Provide a chart with enough low columns for the task: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 needs a ten-thousandths column, so the chart should extend beyond thousandths for the division example.
Recognition and fill-in tasks check fluency but do not by themselves build the shift image; pair them with enacted chart work.

Discussion/dialogue activities can surface and challenge misconceptions and can accompany the enacted chart work; they need not be treated as the only route, but the curriculum concept here centres on the learner performing the digit shift.

Paper or card digit cards used on a chart have slight physical thickness and are approximations of the abstract place-value idea; an on-screen chart with sliding digits is a model of the same relationship — both are legitimate ways to enact the shift.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 (each digit two columns left), 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 (three columns right; placeholder 0 in ones by convention and in tenths, final digit in ten-thousandths), 3.456 ÷ 1000 = 0.003456, and 2.5 × 10 = 25 are correct as stated and were checked independently.

The place-value chart must extend to ten-thousandths: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 places its final digit (2) in the ten-thousandths column, so a chart ending at thousandths (as the original representation described) cannot hold the result. Learner text now spans thousands to ten-thousandths.

The stated objective and summary say answers 'up to three decimal places', but the flagship division example 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 yields four decimal places. The arithmetic is correct; this is an original-row inconsistency flagged for review, not a learner error.

The original row's recommendation text said 'three placeholder zeros' fill the vacated ones and tenths places for 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452; that is a slip — only two written zeros are present (the ones leading zero by convention and the tenths placeholder). The learner-facing text uses the corrected 'ones and tenths' (two zeros).

The original row's optional 'drag the point instead' toggle was not carried into learner actions: moving the point and moving the digits give the same relative result only because position is relative, which can confuse learners. It is noted here for reviewers to decide whether to include such a toggle at all.
CCSS-M 5.NBT and NCETM source claims were marked unverified in the original and remain unverified here; no new verification was performed.
The reteach prerequisite links and diagnostic structure from the assessment fields were not altered and are out of scope for this rewrite.

probeDeeper: When you multiplied by 100, did the point move or did the digits move?
Why does 45.2 ÷ 1000 need those zeros after the decimal point?
Explain what multiplying by 10 does to the value of each digit.
Someone wrote 3.45600 for 3.456 × 100. What did they misunderstand?
assess.correctAnswer: 345.6; 0.0452. The teacher watches for each digit shifting two places left (×100) and three places right (÷1000), the decimal point staying fixed while digits move, and placeholder zeros inserted (the leading 0.0452).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'add zeros' / 'remove zeros' rule — 3.456 × 100 becomes 3.45600, value unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: place-value chart: ×100 makes each digit worth 100× more, so digits move two columns LEFT; the point doesn't move, the digits do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer keeps the point fixed among the same digits and appends zeros; magnitude wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: 'move the decimal point' the wrong way or wrong number of places for division
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as digits shifting RIGHT three places for ÷1000; each digit becomes a thousandth of its value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 45.2 ÷ 1000 comes out as 45200 or 4.52 rather than 0.0452

errorPatterns.pattern: forgets placeholder zeros — 45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 (shifts only visible digits)
errorPatterns.nextMove: count every column crossed and put a zero in each empty place, giving 0.0452.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: too few decimal places; leading zeros omitted

errorPatterns.pattern: shifts correctly but miscounts by one place under speed
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; match the number of zeros in the multiplier/divisor to places shifted and recount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a factor of ten; self-corrects on recount

responseLevels.gap: relies on 'add zeros', gives 3.45600, or moves the point the wrong way/amount; no placeholders.
responseLevels.full: shifts digits the correct number of places both ways to 3 d.p., inserts all placeholder zeros, keeps the point fixed, and explains each digit's changed value.
responseLevels.partial: shifts correctly for the multiplication but drops placeholder zeros or mis-shifts on the division to 3 d.p.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they like: 3.456 × 100, then 45.2 ÷ 1000. Watch whether they SHIFT each digit the right number of places (with the point staying put) or fall back on 'add/remove zeros' and 'move the point', and whether they insert placeholder zeros.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: At 3 d.p. the 'add a zero' shortcut clearly breaks (3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600). Watching a division that produces leading zeros (45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) exposes whether the child fills placeholders and understands digits shifting through the place-value chart rather than manipulating the point by a half-remembered rule.
